body:
We have 725 `GLOBAL_GET` currently in `master`.

Is there any downside to making the cached version the default behavior so we don't have to decide on a case by case basis to use `GLOBAL_GET_CACHED`? (I assume we'll need to include the type info anyway so all 725 occurrences would need to be updated, but at least we could do this once and for all).

I agree we should probably make `GLOBAL_GET()` cached by default, and have uncached behavior in a separate macro like `GLOBAL_GET_NO_CACHE()`. This may lead to slight breakage in third-party modules though.

Also, should editor settings also get a similar treatment? Situations where editor settings are queried more frequently than needed are probably less common than for project settings.

> Situations where editor settings are queried more frequently than needed are probably less common than for project settings.

Call it a hunch, but I feel like while it _is_ less common, the settings are accessed much more frequently.

> I agree we should probably make `GLOBAL_GET()` cached by default

I agree too, but wouldn't that also mean that existing code, aware of the macro's lack of cache, should be removed? There's no reason for both caches to coexist, I assume?

It's likely a bit more than 4 bytes with the static std::mutex (seems to vary by OS but might be 40-80 bytes).

> Is there any downside to making the cached version the default behavior so we don't have to decide on a case by case basis to use GLOBAL_GET_CACHED?

We can't use the cached version _as is_ with `String`, `Variant` or complex types like `Dictionary` or `Array` (i.e. we've statically asserts trivally destructible).

The reason is that, as with Coverity scans, it isn't safe to use these types with static lifetime, because their construction / destruction relies on other machinery which is also static lifetime, and thus falls foul of the "static initialization order fiasco". In some cases the machinery may not be static but might be created after / destroyed before statics.

Some alternate versions we discussed might not have this restriction on other types, like passing a pointer to a local struct containing the whole `value, version, mutex`, but there is no guarantee the contributor wouldn't try and use this with static lifetime (there's no easy way of checking this in c++), and it is introducing boilerplate, and the point of the PR is not to introduce additional boiler plate.

An alternative could be to put an `if constexpr std::is_trivially_destructible` in the macro, so it automatically uses the old version (but only if the compiler can figure this out and optimize out the statics etc, which is unlikely without some macro-fu). But it's semantically vague, the user might think the value is cached when it is not.

We did talk about possibly changing the naming convention in the 3.x PR, in terms of having the cached version be `GET_GLOBAL` and the old version be `GET_GLOBAL_UNCACHED`, but haven't swapped it over yet.

> I agree too, but wouldn't that also mean that existing code, aware of the macro's lack of cache, should be removed? There's no reason for both caches to coexist, I assume?

No, it is more efficient (and recommended) to cache values locally using either `project_settings_changed` signal or a NOTIFICATION or calling `ProjectSettings::has_changes()` each frame and calling your own function that updates all your local project settings caches. I notice now that 4.x doesn't seem to have `has_changes()` yet but I believe you have your own version of `project_settings_changed` signal?

`GET_GLOBAL_CACHED` is the lazy approach, because it involves a a branch and mutex _every time_ for something that should ideally not be checked, it is better updated in a push fashion.

This is partly why Juan queried the approach because he knew developers are lazy and are less likely to do it "properly". :grin: 

But it is a "damned if you do", "damned if you don't" situation. It's usually enough that every now and then optimization guys come in and make sure the hot project settings are updated in the efficient way. There is already afaik a mega function in the `EditorNode` that updates a whole load of project settings the best way - yup `NOTIFICATION_EDITOR_SETTINGS_CHANGED`.

It's kind of like at the moment:
```
Respond to signal / notification / has_changes() - cost 0
GLOBAL_GET_CACHED - cost 10
GLOBAL_GET - cost 500
```

After some benchmarking today, we agreed to change `Mutex` to `SpinLock`. 2x as fast (on my Linux), and the likelihood of contention is very low as these are local `SpinLocks` (so several threads would need to be running the same function at once).

Additionally memory used by `SpinLock` is (potentially) a lot less, although there is an alignment hack currently in `SpinLock`.

Also prefixed all variables with `_ggc_` because compiler is set to report shadowed variables (and these can be in the surrounding code outside the lambda).
Do we need an `EDITOR_GET_CACHED` as well to apply the same optimizations with the editor settings?
Mhm! It's been considered, but it's less "urgent" because at least `EDITOR_GET` doesn't affect a released project.

I found this issue while tracking down another battery burning code path in the editor (part of the ongoing saga from https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/116845), and found that SceneTree was not updated to use the GLOBAL_GET_CACHED because it uses a string - no problem, the fix is simple.   But that particular code in SceneTree does a lot of additional and needless work on each tick [1]

It feels to me that the reason why we need GLOBAL_GET_CACHED in the first place is that Godot does not offer a convenient system to express "I need to track Project-level settings", so the tool that folks are reaching out to is to probe and update state live during these time ticks that are a precious resource.

GLOBAL_GET_CACHED provided a spot solution to an endemic problem, the right solution would be to provide a convenient solution to every consumer of these tokens and eliminate every instance where the changes are done dynamically on a per-frame handler.   In fact, we could go as far as having a system to register these changes, something like:

```
TRACK_USAGE("audio/general/3d_panning_strength", panning_strenght_changed)
```

And we could then disable both GLOBAL_GET and GLOBAL_GET_CACHED altogether, their use would be an indicator that something is off.

[1] The localized patch I am using (4.5-based patch) for the scene tree case: https://gist.github.com/migueldeicaza/b0607cbddd13a2e00107eb65d85d3f70

There is a way to track settings: the `settings_changed` signal and `check_changed_settings_in_group()` method.

> TRACK_USAGE("audio/general/3d_panning_strength", panning_strenght_changed)

`panning_strenght_changed` is a callback? Having a method for every single setting is going to bloat the code more than necessary.

> And we could then disable both GLOBAL_GET

How are you going to get a setting value then, even to update it when changed?

The callback should receive the new value that was set as an argument.

Bloat-wise the amount of instructions changes are likely negligible and are offset by not having that inlined GLOBAL_GET_CACHED macro today[1], and we would eliminate all that code from the process handlers which tends to be sprinkled as sparking side effects, when what it is really doing is giving the illusion of instant changes.

[1]
```
#define GLOBAL_GET_CACHED(m_type, m_setting_name) ([](const char *p_name) -> m_type {\
static_assert(std::is_trivially_destructible<m_type>::value, "GLOBAL_GET_CACHED must use a trivial type that allows static lifetime.");\
static m_type _ggc_local_var;\
static uint32_t _ggc_local_version = 0;\
static SpinLock _ggc_spin;\     
uint32_t _ggc_new_version = ProjectSettings::get_singleton()->get_version();\
if (_ggc_local_version != _ggc_new_version) {\
        _ggc_spin.lock();\
        _ggc_local_version = _ggc_new_version;\
        _ggc_local_var = ProjectSettings::get_singleton()->get_setting_with_override(p_name);\
        m_type _ggc_temp = _ggc_local_var;\
        _ggc_spin.unlock();\
        return _ggc_temp;\
}\
_ggc_spin.lock();\
m_type _ggc_temp2 = _ggc_local_var;\
_ggc_spin.unlock();\
return _ggc_temp2; })(m_setting_name)
```
